analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and their spouses from owning or trading stocks and securities.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan ban, with 29 House cosponsors from both parties, never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar members of Congress and their spouses from owning or trading any stock, bond, commodity, future, or security, including hedge funds and derivatives. Current and new members would have 180 days to divest (five years for complex private-fund holdings), with exceptions for diversified index funds, government retirement plans, Treasury bonds, and certain small-business holdings. Violations would carry fines of up to $50,000 each, and members would not owe capital gains tax on a required divestment if they reinvested in permitted funds within 60 days.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans who want lawmakers making policy on issues like tariffs, subsidies, and industry regulation without a personal financial stake in the companies those decisions move. Members' constituents gain a clearer guarantee that congressional votes are not influenced by members' own portfolios.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits members of Congress and their spouses from owning or trading any stock, bond, commodity, future, or other security, including hedge-fund and derivative positions, removing the potential conflict between lawmakers' personal portfolios and their legislative work.

Requires divestment within 180 days for current and new members, and within 180 days for assets received during service such as an inheritance, so the ban takes effect quickly rather than allowing indefinite holding.
Imposes a civil fine of up to $50,000 for each violation, enforceable by the Attorney General or the Special Counsel, putting a real financial penalty behind the ban.
Lets members divest without recognizing capital gains tax if they buy permitted bonds or diversified funds within 60 days, easing the cost of complying with the ban.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their spouses, who would have to sell individual securities and move their money into diversified funds, Treasury bonds, or retirement accounts. Members holding private hedge-fund or venture-capital interests would have up to five years to unwind them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their spouses

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves significant channels open: spouses may still trade securities in the course of their own primary occupation, and members may hold interests in small businesses that do not present a defined conflict of interest, so a member could still have financial exposure to policy areas through a spouse's or family's business.

The maximum penalty of $50,000 per violation is small relative to the wealth of many members, and enforcement depends on the Attorney General or Special Counsel choosing to sue; the bill creates no dedicated independent enforcer.

Members get five years to divest hedge-fund, venture-capital, and other privately held complex vehicles, a much longer runway than the 180 days given to ordinary securities, and receive a tax break on divestiture proceeds.

A good-faith objection is that a full ownership ban, rather than disclosure or conflict recusal rules, may make it harder for wealthy candidates to serve or may simply push members' assets into less-visible family arrangements, since the bill only covers members and their spouses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large and easy to state: lawmakers would no longer be able to hold or trade individual stocks while legislating on the companies those stocks represent. The exceptions for spouses' occupational trading, small-business stakes, and slow divestment of private funds mean the ban is not airtight, and the $50,000 fine is modest. Still, the exemptions are narrow and the mechanism is straightforward, so the bill's design would deliver substantially more integrity benefit than cost, with the main cost falling on the lawmakers themselves.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with bipartisan sponsors and referred to four House committees, but none of them ever held a markup, and the bill never came to a vote in the House or Senate before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the bill on March 21, 2023, with an initial group of cosponsors that included Democrats such as Reps. DeLauro, Nadler, Porter, and Auchincloss and Republicans Reps. Buck and Rosendale.
The bill was referred to four committees at once — Financial Services, Agriculture, House Administration, and Ways and Means — meaning any of them could have acted on it.
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action after the initial referral, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the bill ever advancing.
In total, 29 House members cosponsored the bill: 21 of 216 House Democrats and 8 of 224 House Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress who hold or trade individual stocks came out ahead: the ban never advanced, and the current disclosure-based rules remained in place for the rest of the Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress who trade stocks

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — 21 of 216 House Democrats and 8 of 224 House Republicans cosponsored, and two Republicans were original cosponsors — but the bill never reached a vote, so no party split was ever recorded on it.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and their spouses
industries.note: By the bill dying, sitting members keep the ability to own and trade individual stocks and securities while legislating on the companies involved, subject only to the existing disclosure rules. The rules the bill would have replaced are written by the same people they would govern.
